messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: triangle distribution problems + fmax, fabs
parts:
I tested the uniform distribution, and it works
just fine into the corners with NUTS with or without
declared bounds (i.e., transforms) on the variable.
The untransformed case runs much more slowly, probably
due to smaller step sizes.

Untransformed variables (1K adapt, 1K samples):

0% 2.5% 10% 25% 50% 90% 97.5% 100%
0.0018 0.0244 0.0946 0.2430 0.4878 0.8843 0.9842 0.9989

Transformed variables (same conditions):

0% 2.5% 10% 25% 50% 90% 97.5% 100%
0.0029 0.0261 0.0988 0.2770 0.5281 0.8961 0.9753 0.9992


It's a different story for the triangle. Here's the model:

src/models/triangle.stan
------------------------
parameters {
double(-1,1) y;
}
model {
lp__ <- lp__ + log(fmax(0.0,1.0 - fabs(y)));
}
---------------------

The fmax() just makes sure we get -infinity
rather than NaN for probabilities of points
outside of [-1,1].

I have bounded y to be (-1,1), which works just
fine. If I remove the bound, it doesn't sample
the corners well.

Transformed variable (same conditions):

0% 2.5% 10% 25% 50% 90% 97.5% 100%
-0.992 -0.758 -0.522 -0.269 0.008 0.526 0.769 0.954

Untransformed variable (ditto):

0% 2.5% 10% 25% 50% 90% 97.5% 100%
-0.858 -0.803 -0.504 -0.301 0.033 0.557 0.746 0.782

The quantiles for the transformed-variable samples are right,
but the untransformed ones are too thin on the tails.

============ bonus section: fmax and fabs() =========================

I used the C++ lib functions fmax() and fabs()
instead of the C++ lib functions because max() and abs()
because the latter have undefined behavior for
floating point (they were originally only for int
types). Some of the bugs in our distributions were
from using abs() where we should've used fabs().

It's ugly, but the alternative is a layer of
C++-to-Stan function aliasing, which I'd rather stay
away from if I can manage (though with user extensions
and required namespaces in names, I may decide it's
the lesser of two evils at some later point). The main
reason is that I've always found renaming layers (as in
J2EE) to be very confusing. The secondary reason is that
it means less coding and hence less doc and less maintenance.

- Bob
